Universities

How to Shortlist Universities and Courses Without Feeling Overwhelmed

By Achieve Aboard Team·2 October 2026·2 min read

In this article

  1. Step 1: Choose your top three priorities
  2. Step 2: Build a longlist of eight to ten options
  3. Step 3: Check the basics for each option
  4. Step 4: Look at what happens inside the course
  5. Step 5: Consider student support and campus life
  6. Step 6: Cut your list to three to five
  7. A simple comparison table
  8. Want a second pair of eyes?

There are a lot of universities and courses to choose from. The trick is to narrow the field in stages, rather than comparing everything at once.

Step 1: Choose your top three priorities

Decide what matters most: a particular course, a budget limit, a destination, a start date, or a scholarship opportunity. Having three clear priorities makes every later decision easier.

Step 2: Build a longlist of eight to ten options

Search by course and country, and note down every option that looks interesting. At this stage you are collecting, not deciding.

Step 3: Check the basics for each option

For every university on your list, note down:

  • The exact course name and level
  • Entry requirements, including English language requirements
  • Course length and intake months
  • Annual tuition fees and estimated living costs
  • Application deadlines

Step 4: Look at what happens inside the course

Two courses with similar names can be very different. Read the course structure, modules, assessment style and any practical or work-based components. Check whether the course suits the career or further study you have in mind.

Step 5: Consider student support and campus life

Look for support services for international students, such as orientation programs, accommodation help and academic support. These matter a great deal in your first months abroad.

Step 6: Cut your list to three to five

Remove options that do not meet your top priorities or that you may not qualify for. Keep a mix: a couple that are your top choices and one or two that feel like sensible backups.

A simple comparison table

Make a table with one row per university and these columns: course, country, tuition per year, entry requirements, intake, deadline and notes. Seeing everything side by side often makes the best choice obvious.
